cosy-lesson.title: Why Do We Feel Empty After Finishing a Series?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Mourn – feel or show deep sorrow or regret for someone or something.

p.em: Example: It is completely natural to mourn the conclusion of a drama that felt so real.

cosy-blockquote.p: Bereavement – the deep sadness felt after losing a close friend or relative.

p.em: Example: The sudden departure of our favorite characters can feel like a miniature bereavement.

cosy-blockquote.p: Parasocial – relating to a one-sided relationship with a media figure who doesn't know you exist.

p.em: Example: We form parasocial bonds with actors because we witness their most intimate moments.

cosy-blockquote.p: Binge-watch – watch many episodes of a TV show one after another in a short time.

p.em: Example: When you binge-watch a drama, you merge your timeline with theirs.

cosy-blockquote.p: Emptiness – the state of containing nothing, or a feeling of lack of meaning.

p.em: Example: A profound emptiness washed over her as the final credits rolled.

cosy-blockquote.p: Catharsis – the healthy release of strong feelings to feel better and relaxed.

p.em: Example: Watching the finale provided a deep sense of emotional catharsis for the audience.

cosy-blockquote.p: Escapism – the practice of escaping real-life problems by seeking entertainment.

p.em: Example: Our favorite television serial serves as a perfect piece of harmless escapism.

cosy-blockquote.p: Melancholy – a soft, gentle feeling of sadness without any clear reason.

p.em: Example: The dark living room was filled with a quiet melancholy after the final episode.

cosy-blockquote.p: Companionship – fellowship or the state of having a companion.

p.em: Example: Fictional figures offer a weirdly stable form of companionship in lonely times.

cosy-blockquote.p: Interweave – blend closely together or connect in an intricate way.

p.em: Example: Our daily routines interweave with the narratives we follow every single night.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
Why is it that we can mourn fictional characters as if they were people we shared meals with?
★ Have you ever shed actual tears during a television finale?

Does the ending of a long-running show trigger a genuine sense of bereavement in modern audiences?
★ What is the hardest goodbye you have ever had to say to a television show?

How do parasocial relationships help us navigate moments of social isolation in big cities?
★ Have you ever felt more understood by a fictional character than by your real-life friends?

Does our tendency to binge-watch intensify the emotional crash when we finally run out of episodes?
★ Do you prefer to watch a show weekly or consume it all in one sitting?

What is the psychological root of the sudden emptiness we feel when our favorite fictional world shuts its gates?
★ How do you usually fill the quiet void left by a finished series?

Why does a tragic ending sometimes offer a cleaner sense of catharsis than a happy, predictable one?
★ What is a television show ending that completely frustrated or disappointed you?

Is television escapism a healthy coping mechanism or a dangerous shield from real-world responsibilities?
★ Do you use television to escape from stressful days?

Why does the quiet melancholy of a rainy Sunday perfectly match the mood of finishing a heavy season?
★ Does the weather outside affect the types of series you choose to watch?

Can fictional companionship ever replace the messiness of real human connections?
★ Who is your favorite fictional best friend from any television show?

How do writers masterfully interweave complex human flaws to make us fall in love with problematic heroes?
★ Have you ever found yourself rooting for a character who was technically a villain?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
Older generations had to actively mourn physical losses, while modern audiences experience a synthetic grief over fictional characters.
★ Have you ever felt a genuine, deep sadness when a fictional character died?

We experience a modern post-series bereavement because we lack the real-life neighborhood bonds that previous generations enjoyed.
★ Have you ever watched a show alone and wished you had someone to talk about it with?

Modern parasocial relationships with digital characters are a poor substitute for the active, shared community life of our ancestors.
★ Do you prefer to watch a series week-by-week or binge it all at once?

The modern urge to binge-watch entire stories in a weekend leaves us with an immediate emotional void that older, slower serials avoided.
★ Do you find yourself forgetting the plots of shows you watched just a few months ago?

Traditional societies filled their lives with enduring, shared myths, whereas modern citizens use endless TV shows to escape existential emptiness.
★ What is a book, movie, or myth that has permanently shaped your worldview?

Older storytellers offered a live, communal catharsis, while modern streaming has isolated us in highly personal emotional vacuums.
★ Does having too many entertainment choices ever make you feel anxious or bored?

We use constant media escapism to avoid the raw challenges of real life, a distraction our ancestors were too busy to afford.
★ Do you prefer reading books or watching screen adaptations to spark your imagination?

Older generations accepted narrative endings as final, while modern consumerism stretches stories indefinitely, leaving us in a state of perpetual melancholy.
★ Are you frustrated when a favorite series is dragged on for too many seasons?

We seek a synthetic companionship through high-definition screens, trading the messy warmth of real human interactions for safe, curated dramas.
★ How patient are you when waiting for a new season of a show you love?

Modern entertainment algorithms interweave commercial data with our emotional desires, controlling what we watch and feel in ways the past never knew.
★ Do you think an algorithm can truly understand your artistic taste?
